Jarir pledged allegiance to the Prophet to testify that none is worshipped but Allah and Muhammad is His Apostle, pray, pay zakat, listen and obey, and advise every Muslim well.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans before they reach market, town dwellers acting as brokers for desert dwellers, and reselling food bought from caravans before carrying it to market.
Barirah's masters insisted on her wala', but the Prophet told Aisha to buy her, as wala' belongs to the one who frees and conditions not in Allah's Book are invalid.
Wheat for wheat, barley for barley and dates for dates are riba unless equal in amount and handed over hand to hand.
The Prophet forbade Muzabana, selling fresh dates or grapes for dried ones by measure, or unmeasured fruit against a measured amount, but allowed selling fruit on trees by estimation.
Gold for gold, silver for silver, must be equal and hand to hand, else riba; gold for silver is allowed, not on credit; Ibn Abbas saw riba only in delay.
Dates may not be sold before safe from blight, nor fresh for dried; Muzabana and Muhaqala are forbidden, but 'Araya owners may sell fruit by estimate, up to five wasqs.
Fruit may not be sold before its benefit is evident, red or yellow, fit to eat, for if Allah spoils it the seller has no right to the buyer's money.
The Prophet bought foodstuff on credit from a Jew and pledged his armour to him.
Learning Khaibar's governor bartered one sa of fine dates for two, the Prophet forbade it as a kind of usury: sell the mixed dates for money, then buy good ones.
Fruits of sold pollinated palms go to the seller unless the buyer stipulates them; Muzabana and similar sales are forbidden, as is selling dates before they turn red or yellow.
Eating fresh dates, the Prophet says one tree resembles a faithful believer; Ibn Umar, the youngest present, kept quiet, and the Prophet names the date palm.
Abu Taiba, a slave, cupped the Prophet, who ordered him paid a Sa of dates and ordered his masters to reduce his tax.
Hind says Abu Sufyan is a miser, and the Prophet lets her and her sons take from his money what is sufficient, reasonably and fairly.
Aisha says verse 4.6 came about the guardian of orphans: a rich guardian takes no wages from their property, a poor one what is just and reasonable for his labour.
The Prophet gave pre-emption in every joint undivided property, but none once the boundaries are marked and the ways and streets fixed.
Three men shut in a cave by a rock each invoke Allah by a deed done for His sake, and the rock moves away bit by bit.
The Prophet asks a pagan driving sheep whether they are for sale or a gift, and buys one sheep from him.
Abraham, emigrating with Sarah, calls her his sister before a tyrant king; her prayers leave the king seized whenever he approaches, and he sends her back with a slave-girl.
A disputed boy goes to Abd bin Zam'a, the child belonging to the bed's owner, though Sauda screens herself; Suhaib, told to claim only his father, says he was kidnapped.
Hakim bin Hizam asks about the kin ties he kept, slaves he freed and alms he gave before Islam, and the Prophet says he embraced Islam with those good deeds.
Passing a dead sheep, the Prophet says its skin could be used, for only eating it is unlawful.
The son of Mary will soon descend as a just ruler, break the Cross, kill the pig and abolish the Jizya; money will then abound and none will accept charity.
Umar curses a seller of alcohol, citing the curse on Jews who sold fat forbidden to them; picture-makers will be punished, and the alcohol trade was made unlawful.
Allah will be against three on Resurrection Day: one who betrays a covenant made in His name, one who sells a free person, and one who withholds a labourer's wages.
Safiya, a captive, was given to Dihya Al-Kalbi, then the Prophet; asked about coitus interruptus with captives, he says it is better not to, as every destined soul will exist.
The Prophet sold a Mudabbar on behalf of his master, who was still living and in need of money.
An unmarried slave-girl proved guilty of illegal sexual intercourse is flogged each time, without further blame, and sold on the third or fourth offence, even for a hair rope.
After Khaibar was conquered the Prophet chose Safiya, whose husband had been killed, married her on the way with a wedding meal of Hais, and helped her mount his camel.

In Mecca's conquest year the Prophet forbids trading alcohol, carcasses, pigs and idols; he forbade a dog's price, money for blood, prostitutes' and soothsayers' earnings, and cursed tattooing and Riba.
Finding Medina's people paying in advance for fruit delivered years later, the Prophet says advance payment must be for a known measure, a known weight and a known period.
Ibn Abi Aufa and Ibn Abza say the companions paid in advance for wheat, barley, raisins and oil of known measure and period, without asking Sham's peasants about crops.
Asked about advance payment for dates, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar say the Prophet forbade selling dates until fit to eat; Ibn Umar adds silver for gold on credit.
The Prophet bought foodstuff from a Jew on credit for a set period and mortgaged his iron armour to him.
Advance payment for fruit is for a fixed measure and period; companions paid Sham peasants in advance without asking about crops; and sale timed by a she-camel's birth is forbidden.
The Prophet ruled pre-emption (Shuf'a) for every undivided joint property, but none once the limits are marked and the ways and streets fixed.
Abu Rafi sells his dwellings to Sa'd below another offer, as the Prophet said a neighbour has more right for his nearness; gifts go first to the nearest door.
An honest treasurer is one of two charitable persons; no post goes to one demanding it; the Prophet shepherded for pay, and he and Abu Bakr hire a pagan guide.
A man who bit another's finger lost his own tooth, and the Prophet, and Abu Bakr in a similar case, rejected his claim for compensation.
Al-Khadir straightens a wall about to fall with his hand, and Moses says he could have taken wages for it to buy food.
